CNN frames it as the latest evidence that, after a year of letting Kennedy 'go wild,' Trump and his aides are 'shortening the leash' on the HHS secretary ahead of the midterms: installing conventional-background nominees at the CDC and surgeon general's office, pulling back HHS's push to overhaul vaccine policy in favor of issues with wider appeal like drug prices, and siding with agricultural corporations over Kennedy on glyphosate. The most striking line comes from an unnamed Trump adviser, who questioned whether the movement was ever the political force it claimed to be: 'I hate to say it, but I think they're a little bit overrated. To some extent, MAHA has always been a paper tiger.' MAHA leaders pushed back hard. Turning Point USA podcaster Alex Clark, who had personally pressed Trump on Means's confirmation at the April 9 Oval Office meeting, called Saphier's selection 'a catastrophic mistake' and said she 'gets an F when it comes to all things MAHA.' Vani Hari ('Food Babe') argued the administration should leave the post vacant rather than confirm Saphier, and warned: 'This is a fast-growing, highly energized coalition of parents, farmers, and health advocates and we're organizing in ways Washington isn't used to. Ignoring that heading into the midterms is not just wrong, it's politically shortsighted.' The White House disputed any suggestion Kennedy is being sidelined; spokesman Kush Desai said MAHA 'has been a Day One priority' and Kennedy 'continues to play a central role.' CNN notes the open question some in Trump's orbit are now asking: whether MAHA will make the compromises needed to become a durable part of the GOP coalition, or remain, as one adviser put it, a 'factional offshoot on the political fringe.' Arizona GOP strategist Barrett Marson raised the inverse risk for Republicans: 'I think the right candidate, either a Democrat or Republican, could win MAHA voters with a message that they would want to hear.'

title: Trump Administration Shelves Black Lung Silica Rule as Miners Get Sick and Die
description: The Trump administration has shelved a 2024 MSHA rule that would have brought silica dust limits in coal mines down from 100 to 50 micrograms per cubic meter; the compliance window was due to open in April 2025. Unlike coal dust, silica particles embed in lung tissue and trigger irreversible scarring with no treatment. The condition now hits 1 in 10 miners with 25 or more years underground and is reaching workers in their 30s and 40s. MSHA's workforce has simultaneously contracted, with 90 newly hired inspectors losing their positions. This comes as the administration signed an executive order naming coal a national security priority. "If the Trump administration actually cared about protecting coal miners from black lung, we'd have a strong silica rule in place right now," said Rebecca Shelton of the Appalachian Citizens' Law Center. "Instead, they are hiding behind a ridiculous legal process to delay action while miners get sick and die."

title: Trump EPA Moves to Repeal EtO Cancer Protections, Curtailing Future Regulatory Authority
description: The Trump EPA moved to strike down 2024 regulations on ethylene oxide (EtO), a carcinogenic gas used to sterilize 20 billion medical devices annually and linked to leukemia. Recent research found EtO is 60 times more carcinogenic than 2006 estimates; the Biden rule required a 90% emissions cut across 89 facilities. Repealing it would leave 2.3 million people, disproportionately in working-class and low-income communities, breathing nearly 8 tons of the gas each year, while saving industry $47 million annually. No accounting for the resulting cancer burden has been produced. The deeper legal problem: the administration is arguing the Clean Air Act does not authorize discretionary risk reviews beyond the first mandatory one, permanently curtailing the EPA's ability to update protections as new science emerges. "This sends up a signal flare to everyone that we've got a real threat, and that the administration plans to gut cancer protections," said Erik Olson of the NRDC. A Harvard analysis confirms the move is "part of a broader pattern of authority-limiting interpretations by the EPA" under this administration.

title: Trump Forces Out FDA Commissioner Makary; RFK Jr.'s Spokesperson Resigns in Protest
description: Trump forced out FDA Commissioner Marty Makary on May 12 after months of friction over his resistance to approving fruit-flavored e-cigarettes and his refusal to restrict mifepristone. Trump said only that Makary "was having some difficulty," without specifying whether he fired or requested his resignation. The following day, Rich Danker, RFK Jr.'s chief HHS spokesperson, submitted his own resignation letter citing concerns about "approval of e-cigarette flavors that would appeal to children and expose them to nicotine addiction, lung damage, and higher risk of cancer." Kyle Diamantas, the FDA's deputy food commissioner, was named acting commissioner.

title: Big Tobacco Buys an FDA Policy: Executives Dine with Trump, Vaping Rules Reversed Within a Week
description: A New York Times investigation published May 13 documents the direct line from tobacco industry money to an FDA policy reversal. On May 3, President Trump lunched with tobacco executives and lobbyists at his Jupiter, Fla. golf club — including top officials from Reynolds American and Altria, and lobbyist Brian Ballard, a major Trump fundraiser whose firm has been paid more than $4.4 million by Reynolds since 2017. When the executives complained about FDA vaping rules, Trump interrupted to call Commissioner Makary on the spot. No answer. He then called RFK Jr. and Dr. Oz directly to register his displeasure. Less than a week later, the FDA issued guidance opening the door to flavored vape sales — bypassing the scientific review process the agency had defended up to the Supreme Court. Makary resigned rather than sign off. The donation trail is unambiguous: Reynolds gave $10 million to a Trump super PAC during the 2024 campaign and $3 million more after his win; Altria gave $1 million to the inaugural and $1 million to a super PAC; the Vapor Technology Association gave $1.25 million to the inaugural; Reynolds and Altria each donated to Trump's proposed White House ballroom fundraiser and their executives attended the $2.5 million-per-donor dinner. Trump referred to Reynolds officials as "my tobacco guys." The administration's position: "The only guiding factor behind the Trump administration's health policymaking is gold standard science."

title: WaPo Editorial Reframes Makary's Firing as Deregulatory Opportunity, Amplifying Industry Talking Points
description: A Washington Post opinion piece framed Makary's forced exit as "a much-needed opportunity to reset" the FDA, urging a "more constructive relationship with medical innovators" and warning the next commissioner to "tread carefully when telling Americans what they can eat." On youth vaping, the piece dismissed child health concerns by claiming Makary's resistance to flavored e-cigarette approvals reflected "heavy-handed bans" that "only created a more dangerous black market" — a standard tobacco industry argument that research does not support; flavor restrictions consistently reduce youth use. Food and agriculture journalist Helena Bottemiller Evich called the piece "truly baffling," noting the factual premise that FDA needed reining in was unfounded: "FDA has not issued a single new food regulation during this administration. FDA has not banned a single food chemical during this administration. FDA has not banned a single food product during this administration."

title: Washington Post: The Long-Ignored Science of SSRI Withdrawal, Now Caught in Kennedy's Political War
description: Reporter Ariana Eunjung Cha offers something the May 2026 SSRI debate has mostly lacked: a piece that takes seriously both the value these medications have for millions of people (Cha notes that SSRIs help millions "regain stability") and the patient experience of discontinuation that the medical establishment spent years minimizing. The science shows that experiences coming off them vary widely. Cha's piece centers on those for whom stopping proved far harder than they were ever told it would be, and on how that difficulty was explained away rather than studied. Drug companies for years characterized discontinuation symptoms as typically mild and brief, and rebranded the phenomenon as something other than withdrawal, what researcher Mark Horowitz calls "industry euphemisms." The clinical reality for some patients was quite different, and it went largely undocumented because nobody was looking. Horowitz turned to the research after his own experience stopping SSRIs in his early 20s: "my life kind of exploded," he told the Post. "I was trapped on the drug." What he found was a pharmacological explanation for why some patients struggle most at the very end of a taper, when clinicians and patients alike assume the worst is behind them. His 2019 paper in Lancet Psychiatry on this dose-response dynamic drove a revision of UK clinical guidelines; US guidance has barely moved. Yale psychiatrist Gerard Sanacora identifies a separate systemic failure: the medical system has almost no mechanism for reassessing whether someone still needs a prescription. Stable patients get automatic renewals, and the therapy alternatives that might make medication unnecessary are costlier and harder to access. "It's really not so much an issue of overuse," Sanacora told Cha. "It's an issue of appropriate and inappropriate use." Patient Michael Bosco, 36, on antidepressants since age 8, tried twice to stop under standard medical advice before finding Horowitz's slower protocol. "I don't think people understand you don't have a life if you do it the wrong way," he said. Awais Aftab of Case Western Reserve names the trap Kennedy has now sprung: "the gap in scientific knowledge has allowed a kind of polarized discourse. Some people dismiss them, and others try to exaggerate them, turning them into a panic." The piece does not say Kennedy is wrong that discontinuation deserves more attention. It implies, without quite stating it, that his arrival has turned a real but manageable clinical gap into a political flashpoint, which is the last thing patients navigating a difficult taper actually need.

title: NYT Well: What Psychiatrists Actually Say About Stopping Antidepressants
description: Dana G. Smith's practical piece for the NYT Well section appeared the day Kennedy's summit dominated health coverage and reads as a quiet rebuttal to the political framing around it. Rather than debating overprescribing, Smith asked practicing psychiatrists what the clinical guidance actually says. Their answers are more cautious and individualized than anything Kennedy offered. Experts stress that SSRIs are safe drugs with few serious health risks, that the decision to stop is highly personal, and that the key factors are relapse history, life circumstances, and whether the patient genuinely feels like themselves again. The piece is useful on a specific question the policy debate has largely blurred: how to tell withdrawal from returning illness. "Depression tends to return insidiously over a period of weeks or months, whereas withdrawal symptoms come in with a bang almost immediately," said David Taylor, a professor of psychopharmacology at King's College London. And for patients who have found a medication that works, Taylor's closing note is worth keeping: "If they found a medication that allows them to have a happy life and a productive life, then with some minor exceptions and with some caution, those people probably should continue — because a relapse could be disastrous."Laura Delano, a prominent voice in the antidepressant withdrawal advocacy space, responded on X with a point-by-point critique that accepted the piece's value but challenged several of its underlying claims. She noted that the 'very safe' characterization of SSRIs rests on clinical trials typically lasting six to eight weeks, not the years or decades millions of patients take them. On tapering, she was direct: the piece's 25-percent-per-week protocol is "essentially cold turkey, and incredibly dangerous" for many patients, because the medical profession has not been trained in safe hyperbolic tapering and routinely misdiagnoses withdrawal as relapse as a result. She also challenged the relapse statistics the article cites: withdrawal symptoms are "routinely misclassified as relapse," she wrote, making it difficult to determine who actually has a chronic condition warranting indefinite medication use.

title: NYT Magazine: The Critical Psychiatry Movement That Found an Unlikely Ally in the Trump Administration
description: Daniel Bergner, writing for the NYT Magazine, gives the critical psychiatry movement the most serious intellectual treatment it has received in mainstream coverage of the Kennedy era. Rather than framing the May 4 summit as a political stunt or a MAHA curiosity, Bergner traces the decades-long intellectual genealogy of reform — from the 1980 DSM overhaul that anchored psychiatry to a medical model it was never quite able to prove, through Prozac's promise of effortless recalibration, to the accumulating doubts about whether the chemical imbalance theory that sold the drugs was ever more than a marketing frame. That history is what gives the reform movement its substance, and Bergner treats it as such. The piece centers on Laura Delano and her husband Cooper Davis as the movement's most strategically positioned figures: former psychiatric patient turned activist, now shaping HHS training materials and helping design summit policy documents. Their politics do not map neatly onto the Trump coalition — Delano describes her outlook as "critiquing unchecked, unjust power" — but they have concluded the administration is the most plausible lever for the change they want. The piece is candid about the tensions this creates. Robert Whitaker, whose book Delano credits with redirecting her life, is skeptical that "overmedicalization" framing goes far enough: "I don't think serious reform is enough," he told Bergner. Others in the movement fear the MAHA association taints them as anti-science by proximity to the anti-vax contingent. Awais Aftab, a clinical associate professor at Case Western Reserve who sits closer to the mainstream than most critics, supplied perhaps the piece's sharpest line: "for decades, mainstream psychiatry willfully blinded itself to the burden and severity of withdrawal and discontinuation-related difficulties from antidepressants and other psychiatric medications." Bergner notes two concrete policy outcomes already in motion: CMS will reimburse clinicians for time spent helping patients taper, and HHS will distribute deprescribing training to thousands of practitioners with Delano as a presenter. Whether these gains lead anywhere approaching the transformation the movement envisions is another question. Bergner is clear about what stands in the way: a pharmaceutical industry with the resources to run psychotropic drug ads through every commercial break, and an establishment that has spent fifty years building its authority on the medical model it would now have to abandon.

title: Psychiatry at the Margins: The Szaszian Heart of MAHA Psychiatry
description: Awais Aftab, a psychiatrist who writes at Psychiatry at the Margins, published a pointed response to the Bergner NYT Magazine piece arguing that it obscures what is actually driving the MAHA psychiatric agenda. Bergner frames the movement as a corrective to 1980s reductive psychiatry, but Aftab contends this construction flattens a much larger middle ground: George Engel had already articulated the biopsychosocial model in 1980 alongside the supposed medical model takeover, and most mainstream psychiatry has long operated somewhere between the extremes Bergner describes. The deeper problem, he argues, is that Bergner treats Thomas Szasz as a fringe figure when Szaszian ideas are in fact load-bearing for the movement. The core claim is that mental illness is not pathological, that distress is a life reaction rather than a disorder of biology. In MAHA-adjacent spaces this gets presented through the moderate language of overprescribing and overmedicalization, but the underlying agenda would not survive scrutiny if stated plainly. Aftab characterizes the Whitaker-Moncrieff framework as philosophically and scientifically exhausted: unable to persuade clinical communities through evidence, it has pivoted toward political channels instead. He acknowledges genuine gaps in clinical guidance on antidepressant discontinuation. But on the broader MAHA psychiatric project, he is unsparing, describing the movement as representing the health rhetoric of twenty-first-century American fascism that endangers evidence-based care and public health infrastructure.Two critiques of Aftab's argument are worth holding alongside it. The first is methodological. Aftab treats the alliance between critical psychiatry and MAHA as something to be asserted rather than studied. Biella Coleman, whose chapter "The Politics of Rationality: Psychiatric Survivors' Challenge to Psychiatry" (in Tactical Biopolitics, MIT Press, 2008) traced the psychiatric survivor movement across different eras and political tendencies, has argued that such claims rest on inference rather than the kind of empirical, ethnographic research that would make them defensible. There is a telling contradiction here: Aftab's argument demands evidentiary rigor from psychiatry's critics while making its own social-scientific claims — about who these people are and what drives them — without equivalent grounding. The movement may be exactly what he says it is, or it may be more fractured and contingent; the honest answer is that we do not yet have the data to know. The second critique concerns the fascism charge specifically. Members of this movement are, in many cases, supporting a government that is authoritarian and that many analysts would describe as fascist. But supporting such a government is not the same thing as being fascist oneself — a distinction that matters both analytically and politically, and that Aftab's framing collapses.

title: Laura Delano Responds to the NYT Well Antidepressant Tapering Piece
description: Laura Delano, a public advocate and author who has written extensively about her own psychiatric drug withdrawal, posted a detailed response on X to the NYT Well piece on stopping antidepressants. She commended the Times for covering tapering guidance but challenged five specific claims. The safety characterization rests on clinical trials that typically last six to eight weeks, not the years or decades millions of people are prescribed these drugs. The advice to wait until a patient feels stable before stopping may keep people on medications they are not benefiting from. And the relapse statistics in the piece are compromised at their source: withdrawal symptoms are "routinely misclassified as relapse," she wrote, making it nearly impossible to determine who actually has a chronic condition that warrants indefinite medication use. Her sharpest challenge was to the tapering protocol. The 25-percent-per-week guideline presented as standard clinical practice is, she argued, "essentially cold turkey, and incredibly dangerous" for many patients. Because physicians have not been trained in hyperbolic tapering methods, what clinical settings consider a slow taper can trigger symptoms lasting months or years, which are then misread as relapse. Withdrawal is not merely "uncomfortable," as the article frames it, but can be "life-altering," she wrote, in some cases leading to hospitalization or, in extremes, death.In a separate post, she offered a pointed clarification: "Advocating that people who want to stop their antidepressants are provided with safe, reliable information about tapering off them is not the same thing as advocating that people taper off antidepressants." The distinction matters because critics of the withdrawal advocacy movement routinely conflate the two, treating any push for better discontinuation guidance as covert anti-medication activism.

title: EPA Moves to Repeal Biden PFAS Drinking Water Limits, Drawing Criticism from MAHA Allies
description: The EPA formally proposed repealing drinking water limits for four PFAS compounds and giving utilities more time to comply with limits on two others, unraveling the first new national drinking water standard the agency had successfully set since 1996. The Biden rules, finalized in 2024, were estimated to reduce PFAS exposure for roughly 100 million people. All 50 states have recorded PFAS levels above those standards. The administration's rationale is procedural: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin argued the Biden EPA had rushed the four compounds through without following proper process, leaving the rules legally vulnerable. The two most studied compounds, PFOS and PFOA, will retain their limits, though utilities can apply for a two-year compliance extension. "The science on these two chemicals is some of the strongest on any drinking water contaminant we regulate," Zeldin said. "Those levels are staying." Environmental groups are skeptical even of that concession. The Environmental Working Group and the NRDC argue the rollback likely violates the Safe Drinking Water Act's anti-backsliding provision, which bars the agency from weakening standards once set, and that the extended compliance timeline for PFOS and PFOA may itself run afoul of the law's five-year implementation requirement. The move drew open criticism from within the MAHA coalition, a notable fracture. Conservative wellness influencer and MAHA ally Alex Clark said: "I am tired of making excuses for dangerous chemicals to continue flooding our environment and harming our kids." David Andrews, chief science officer at the Environmental Working Group, was direct: "I don't see how you put a positive light on this. Ultimately, I see this as a betrayal of public health and the mission of making America healthier." Kennedy, who appeared alongside Zeldin at the announcement, highlighted HHS research efforts on PFAS destruction technology but did not defend the rollback directly. When pressed at a congressional hearing in April about EPA actions that appeared to contradict MAHA, he said it was not his department.
